# 8.1 PCA as variance maximisation {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The problem

$X$ is $n \times p$, columns centred and standardised. Seek a unit vector $v_1$ maximising the
variance of the projection:

$$v_1 = \arg\max_{\|v\|=1} \; v^\top \hat\Sigma\, v, \qquad \hat\Sigma = \tfrac{1}{n}X^\top X$$

## The Lagrangian gives an eigenproblem

$$\mathcal{L} = v^\top\hat\Sigma v - \phi(v^\top v - 1)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \hat\Sigma v = \phi v$$

So $v$ must be an **eigenvector** — and since the objective at an eigenvector equals its eigenvalue,
we take the largest.

::: {.muted}
Subsequent components solve the same problem subject to orthogonality to those already found, giving
the eigenvectors in decreasing eigenvalue order.
:::

## Via the SVD

Cleaner, and what software actually computes. With $X = UDV^\top$:

$$\hat\Sigma = \tfrac1n VD^2V^\top$$

::: {.tight}
- **loadings** — the columns of $V$
- **scores** — $Z = XV = UD$
- **variance explained** by component $j$ — $d_j^2/\sum_k d_k^2$
:::

## The connection to Session 05

Ridge shrank along the **same $V$ basis**, damping small-$d_j$ directions.

> **PCA truncates exactly the directions ridge shrinks.**

::: {.check}
Principal components regression is, in this light, a hard-thresholded ridge.
:::

# 8.2 Eckart–Young {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The theorem

Among all matrices of rank $\le k$, the one minimising $\|X - \tilde X\|_F$ is

$$\tilde X_k = U_k D_k V_k^\top$$

the truncated SVD, and the minimum equals $\big(\sum_{j>k} d_j^2\big)^{1/2}$.

## What it licenses you to say

This is the **formal** sense in which "the first $k$ components capture the most information": they
give the best rank-$k$ reconstruction in Frobenius norm.

::: {.check}
It also tells you exactly what you lose — the discarded singular values. Not a heuristic; a
theorem.
:::

# 8.3 The approximate factor model {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Stock and Watson's insight

A large macro panel is well described by a few common shocks plus idiosyncratic noise:

$$X_{it} = \lambda_i^\top F_t + e_{it}, \qquad i = 1,\dots,N,\ t = 1,\dots,T$$

with $F_t \in \mathbb{R}^r$ the common factors and $\lambda_i$ the loadings.

::: {.muted}
The **approximate** factor model (Chamberlain–Rothschild) allows weak cross-sectional and serial
correlation in $e_{it}$ — essential for real data.
:::

## The key result

The principal-component estimator $\hat F_t$ is consistent for the space spanned by $F_t$ as
**both** $N \to \infty$ and $T \to \infty$, at rate $\min(\sqrt N, \sqrt T)$.

::: {.check}
Crucially, if $\sqrt T / N \to 0$, the estimated factors can be treated as **known** in a
second-stage regression — the generated-regressor problem vanishes.
:::

## More series genuinely helps

::: {.warn}
This is the **opposite** of the intuition you built in Sessions 05 and 06, and understanding why is
the heart of this session.
:::

::: {.tight}
- There, extra **predictors** added variance
- Here, extra **measurements of the same latent object** average noise away
:::

## Normalisation

To pin down the rotation, impose

$$F^\top F/T = I_r, \qquad \Lambda^\top\Lambda \text{ diagonal}$$

::: {.warn}
**This is a choice, not a discovery.** Any rotation fits identically well, so "Factor 1" is a
coordinate system — never an object you have found.
:::

# 8.4 How many factors? {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The informal answers

::: {.tight}
- **Scree plot** — look for the elbow. Informal, and often ambiguous.
- **Cumulative variance** — retain enough for 80–90%. Arbitrary but transparent.
:::

## Bai–Ng criteria

Minimise

$$IC_{p1}(k) = \log V(k, \hat F^k) + k\left(\frac{N+T}{NT}\right)\log\left(\frac{NT}{N+T}\right)$$

where $V(k,\hat F^k)$ is the average residual sum of squares from a $k$-factor fit.

::: {.muted}
The penalty must vanish slower than $\min(N,T)^{-1}$. $IC_{p2}$ and $IC_{p3}$ use alternative
penalty forms.
:::

::: {.check}
**Report all three.** If they disagree, say so.
:::

## Cross-checks

::: {.tight}
- **Onatski's test**
- the **eigenvalue-ratio** criterion of Ahn & Horenstein:
  $\hat r = \arg\max_k d_k/d_{k+1}$
:::

::: {.warn}
The course spine was generated from **three** factors. Check what each criterion tells you — and
notice that a criterion can be confidently wrong.
:::

# 8.5 Diffusion-index forecasting {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Two stages

1. Extract $\hat F_t$ by PCA from the standardised, stationary panel of $N$ series.
2. Forecast the target with a small regression on the factors:

$$\hat y_{t+h} = \hat\alpha + \sum_{j=1}^{r}\hat\beta_j \hat F_{jt} + \sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\hat\gamma_\ell y_{t-\ell}$$

## The rule you must not break

> **Factors must be re-estimated at each forecast origin, using only data available at that time.**

::: {.warn}
Extracting factors from the full sample and then backtesting is **look-ahead bias** — and it is the
single most common flaw in student factor-model projects.
:::

::: {.check}
Session 04's rolling-origin discipline applies to **every** step, including the unsupervised one.
:::

# The lab {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## What you do

::: {.tight}
1. Build the wide panel for your angle; standardise it
2. Run PCA; report variance explained and **all three** Bai–Ng criteria
3. Decide $r$ in writing **before** looking at the forecast results
4. Run a diffusion-index forecast, re-estimating factors at each origin
:::

::: {.check}
State your **normalisation** and your **sign convention**. Without them the loadings are not
reproducible.
:::

## The two-minute report

::: {.tight}
1. **What I did** — the panel, the normalisation, how you chose $r$
2. **The number** — variance explained, and forecast error against a benchmark
3. **The catch** — that factors are coordinates, and naming them is an interpretation
:::

::: {.check}
Full brief: [`02-lab/README.md`](02-lab/README.md)
:::
